records.author: ambewas
records.storyText:
I've been developing applications for a long time and have turned to game development as well lately. One of the things that frustrated me the most was that using AI agents for game development is very annoying in the art department. Your only options right now are to either use an image genAI model and roll the dice every time you want to make an edit, or have your agent draw with something like vectors.

I was looking for an application that would allow me to ask an agent to make a first draft of whatever art I needed with actual brushes, and then be able to go in myself and edit every last stroke or layer that it created.

Klad is that application. Written in Rust, it can be fully controlled by an agent through the CLI, and every function is available in a nice UI as well: a brush engine, frame-by-frame animation (and bones/IK), vectors, text layers, colours, layer effects, infinite undo (even after re-opening the file!),…

Why I think it's useful for a wider audience: Adobe showed agents editing Photoshop files at MAX this week, with a private beta planned for early 2027.

Klad is built on the same core idea, with editable paint strokes as core architecture, and it works today.

Clone the repo to try it out: https://github.com/klad-app/klad

You can basically point Claude to the repo, ask it to build it, and pick up the drawing skills. Then ask it to make any drawing you want! (After that, you or the agent can change absolutely every brush stroke in the app again, which makes edits a breeze.)

The quality of the drawings really depends on the agent you use. I have tried it with Claude Fable 5.2 since it came out on Monday, and the drawings are already quite impressive. I'm confident that this will only improve.

I use it every day on Mac, so that definitely works well. It builds on Linux too (tablet pen pressure still needs some work there). Windows builds in CI, I haven't used it there myself yet but I have some reports that it works perfectly fine.

Coming up next is support for pixel art. I'm in the testing phase with this right now, and I expect it to go live in the repo sometime this weekend.

Klad is source-available rather than open source: free to build and use for individuals and small companies, and I plan to sell pre-built binaries later, the way Aseprite does. The file format, CLI reference and agent skill are MIT.

What I want to hear from people who try it: Can your agent work out the CLI without help, and where does it get confused? Can you go in and change one of its strokes easily?

The command reference and guides are available at https://klad.studio

I'll be here answering any questions about the technical side as well, as it's a pretty interesting challenge to build a performant engine with editable brush strokes that render as paint.

records.author: DaleFranks
records.storyText:
I'm new here, and little nervous about posting, but here goes.

I'm not a newbie. I started programming in BASIC when my dad bought home a TRS-80 Model I in 1980, when I was 16. Other than a 9-year stint as active duty military, I've spent 46 years either personally or professionally working in tech. I've programmed in RPG using punch cards for an IBM /System360, and COBOL on a DEC pdp 11/34. I've worked professionally with VB, C#, SQL Server, ColdFusion, PHP, and more. I've seen a lot of technologies come and go. So this ain't the first time I've jogged around this track.

Here's the problem I wanted to solve: I hate WordPress. I mean, as a concept, it's fine, but I used to have a fairly popular motorcycle blog on WP that got trashed by hackers. I've also run into that problem with customers. When hackers find a wordpress site, they just bang on it like a drum. It's a pain. It's also a pain just to manage it, with a wild-west plugin system where plugins constantly fall in and out of compatibility. I'm also not a huge fan of PHP, but since it comes stock with pretty much every shared hosting service, where a lot of my web work is done, it's kind of the default for doing web stuff.

Back in about 2006 or so, I built my own blogging software, which I called .Blog, as an ASP.NET deal in C#. It took me about 6 months to build, start to finish. I didn't have time to keep up with it, which is why I defaulted back to WP sometime around 2014. I migrated to Grav when I ran across it (I guess around 2020 or so), and I liked that. But Grav ran into some issues, and development on it really slowed.

In the past year or so, the company I work for has been delving into using Claude Code, and I got an idea. What if I could just use Claude Code to build a CMS that has everything I want, and nothing I don't?

This project is the result of that idea. I designed the specifications for what I wanted it to do, and let Claude Code handle the actual code writing. I started with a flat-file, markdown-based flat-file CMS, and iterated on that. Fiddling around with markdown files and folders started to get tedious, so I moved towards SQLite as the back-end, to create a system as self-contained and easy to use as possible. This project is, I think, the final result of that idea. This project, from start to finish, took about 2 weeks to build using Laravel/Filament/PHP with Claude Code, compared to the 6 months it took to build .Blog by hand, 20 years ago.

Cripes, I'm old.

Personally, I'm pretty pleased with how this project turned out. I'm running two public websites on it. I'd be interested to hear what others think.

records.title: Show HN: Turri – a coding agent with the power of regenerative software
records.author: ponoru
records.storyText:
Coding agents let me move fast. To keep up, I stopped reading the code, and with it I stopped understanding my own software. I lost my sense of engineering along with it. I was still the one accountable for software I didn't understand. No workflow or better model fixed that, so I built turri.

turri is based on Pi and the concept of regenerative software introduced by Chad Fowler. The ability to regenerate the same piece of code multiple times and always get the same results in terms of functionality is called the deletion test and proves that your coding agent completely understands you. The idea is that every time part of the software needs to be changed, you regenerate a new version of the code based on the durable information you have about the system.

The durable system information includes specs, tests, ADRs, and other types of documents, and it is written in ***plain. You write these with the help of an agent, and Turri starts partial regeneration of the software you're changing. You can repeat this process as many times as you want until you're happy with the change you're implementing. The regeneration also includes proofs that the generated code completely conforms to the system knowledge on which it was based (it implements all the tests that are part of the definition and automatically adds additional tests).

You can try this by cloning the repo or by installing it from my landing page. I created a desktop app to improve usability. Currently, it's only suitable for new projects, but I'm working on adding support for existing projects.

I also wrote the full story in case you're interested: https://turri.dev/blog/why-i-built-turri/

records.title: Show HN: Rebuilding Amazon SES in Rust
records.author: auscaster
records.storyText:
I'm Kam, co-founder and CTO of Nitrosend.

Email is our lifeblood, so we've been gradually moving our email sending onto bare-metal servers and IPs we control.

We wanted to make that move without rewriting the application code already calling Amazon SES. So we built NitroMTA, an open-source SES replacement in Rust. We kept our existing SES v2 sending calls and changed the endpoint and credentials to send through our own engine.

We've been running it in production for a few weeks, moving more mail over as we warm our IPs and build reputation with each mailbox provider.

Keep the SES integration

For an application using boto3, this is the client configuration:

  import boto3
  
  ses = boto3.client(
      "sesv2",
      region_name="us-east-1",
      endpoint_url="https://mail.example.com",
  )
For the SES v2 sending operations we support, the existing calls keep working. We test the official JavaScript, Python and Ruby SDKs against the engine, along with Nodemailer and django-ses. The compatibility page lists the operations and differences from SES: https://nitromta.com/docs/compatibility/

Measuring against KumoMTA and Postfix

In our published 2 November comparison, NitroMTA sustained 3.16 times KumoMTA's throughput and 4.11 times Postfix's. These numbers measure SMTP submission and delivery.

  Engine                Messages per second
  NitroMTA              3,313
  KumoMTA               1,048
  Postfix with OpenDKIM  806
Each engine had four CPU cores and 2 GiB of memory on the same AWS c7gd.metal bare-metal server, with its queue on local NVMe. The workload used 16 KiB messages, authenticated SMTP submission, TLS on submission and delivery, and RSA-2048 DKIM signing. Every engine committed a message to disk before acknowledging it.

The figures are medians of three interleaved runs per engine. The quick profile searches for the highest rate meeting its latency budgets using ten-second load steps, delivering to one receiver site with no added network delay. Across the nine runs, the harness sent 1.35 million messages and checked that each arrived once, with its body intact and its DKIM signature valid.

KumoMTA used its RocksDB spool with set_force_sync(true) to meet the same acceptance contract. KumoMTA documents that this forces database-wide flushes and can substantially reduce performance. The comparison is for that synchronous-acceptance contract; the harness also supports measuring its default asynchronous mode separately.

The method, configurations, exact versions and raw results are published, and you can run the comparison with cargo harness quick: https://nitromta.com/docs/benchmarks/

Give each IP a budget for each provider

An IP needs a sending history with the receivers it sends to. We need to decide how much volume it gets today, what earns it more tomorrow, and what makes us back off.

We track the budget by sending IP and receiver group. That lets us hold an IP's Gmail cap while increasing its cap elsewhere, or lower its Outlook.com cap when Microsoft's responses call for it.

With warmup enabled, the shipped ladder starts at 50 messages a day. A day needs enough SMTP outcomes to test its cap before it earns an increase. Complaints, failures, deferrals and throttling can hold the cap or move it down a rung.

The Outlook.com defaults take fourteen clean daily increases to reach 10,000 messages a day. The default ladder takes seven. Both are configurable.

Before any of this, the host needs outbound port 25 and reverse DNS control for its sending addresses. The domains need SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and bounce and complaint reports need somewhere to arrive. We put the setup checks in nitromta doctor, which prints the missing records.

Provider feedback and durability details continue in a reply.

records.title: Show HN: Daily Atlas, my geography quiz game where rarer answers score more
records.author: ClozeLine
records.storyText:
Hi everyone. I'm an AI Masters student (UvA Amsterdam), and quite the geography nerd, having spent countless hours on GeoGuessr. I wanted to make my own simple geography game, but with some (even small) AI component to it.

The game consists of 6 geography-related questions (countries, capitals, flags, languages, borders, etc) every day, where the rarer your answer, the rarer your score (tiers are [common, uncommon, rare, ultra rare, legendary]). No account needed or anything.

Something I didn't expect to cause so many issues were definitions. What counts as a country? A territory? When does a country 'speak' a language? I would set a definition, and players would always (justifiably so!) break it -> "Well OK then if this is the definition, how come you don't accept [very obscure super borderline answer]". Eventually I converged on a happy-medium with enough inclusion (I think), without the definition being a whole paragraph long:

(i) Country: a sovereign state. Niue and the Cook Islands still cause problems: the UN lists them as "non-member states", but they exhibit quite a bit of sovereignty, so I count them as countries.

(ii) Territory: a place with an ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code, given or reserved, that isn't a sovereign state (e.g., Heard Island and McDonald Islands, Sint Maarten, Sark,...)

(iii) Language spoken in {country}: working or official language, as said so by the government (or the entity's governing body)

Two components I think would be interesting for Show HN, and would like feedback on, are how I determine an answer's rarity and the day's difficulty.

Difficulty: I trained a linear regression model on past play data (30 days, currently) to predict a number between 0 and 1. For each of the first 5 questions (the 6th is different in nature), I gather 3 features for the regression model: ln(num. possible answers), ln(1 + num. 'common' answers), and whether answers contain a 'legandary' (0 or 1), then take the weighted average. Fixed cut-offs snap that into a 1-5 difficulty level (e.g., 4/5).

Rarity (e.g, "Name a country in the EU" -> Belgium):

(i) Fame. Using Google Books Ngram (how often the name appears in English), QRank (pageviews of the name's wikidata item, summed over every wikipedia language), and Wikipedia page views (median yearly views), I calculate a "Fame Score" for every country, territory, and capital (e.g., USA: 7.18, France: 6.85, Tuvalu: 5.76)

(ii) Weight. Sometimes rarities still don't feel quite right, so every question template (e.g., "Name a country in Europe") gets a weight based on how much information it gives the player. Luxembourg is valid for both "Name a country" and "Name a country in Europe", but knowing it's in Europe narrows your possibilities, making Luxembourg an "easier" answer for the latter.

(iii) Multiply Fame times the Weight to get a rarity score from 0-100, snapped to one of the rarity tiers.

It's a side project, and I'm continuously improving things based on feedback from players emailing me. Perhaps some of you could also provide some feedback?

1. How did the game 'feel' to you? 2. Were any of your answers rejected? 3. What is something you like about the game? 4. What is something you dislike about the game? 5. Any other miscellaneous observations/suggestions/bugs

Anything is appreciated. Thank you for your read, and have a good day/night!

records.author: justswim
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I’m Eric and I’m building Lettercamp, an open-source static blog framework. The repo is at https://github.com/lettercamp/lettercamp and the homepage is online at https://www.lettercamp.com.

Writing good content has always been the #1 way that I’ve grown the reach of products I’ve worked on in the past. However, it’s always bothered me how many little things get in the way of writing and publishing high quality, first party content onto the web.

Building a performant, SEO-optimized blog from scratch was always distracting from development on the actual product, and setting up a 3rd party CMS meant that my content always lived in someone else’s database. Storing content in a non-markdown format also made it difficult to draft and edit with the help of an AI agent.

Lettercamp is a modern approach to creating a content site. It ships with all the little features you’d expect in a blog: pagination, authors, metadata, search, cross linking, related posts and more. It’s also statically built, which means that all your content lives in markdown in your codebase, so a deployed version is performant with no database to maintain. This means that you can focus on writing good content instead of vibe-coding a whole blog.

I want to add more features to the framework over time, including better support for AI agents, built in localization, email sign ups, and more.

The repo is released under the MIT license so that anyone can use the framework to create a content site. The goal isn’t to charge individual developers. The monetization path is to provide a cloud hosted version, that has an online editor that content teams can use. The main advantage of this is to decouple the blog from product deploys, so that teams can publish content without needing to push code.

I would love to get your feedback on if this is a problem that might resonate with you or your team. I know that a lot of products create a /blog section at some point, and I wonder what solutions people are using today. My hope is that over time, Lettercamp can be the go-to solution for teams looking to set this up.

Try it out: https://github.com/lettercamp/lettercamp and let me know what you think!

records.title: Show HN: Bot-bottle – secure runtime, DLP and remote control for local agents
records.author: didericis
records.storyText:
Hey! About 6 months ago, I started looking for a tool to safely run coding agents on my (security sensitive) developer machine. Specifically, I wanted a tool that:

- I could use regardless of the model or harness running underneath

- I could build simple, composable, plaintext security policies for

- Provided strong vm level isolation

- Hid credentials from agents

- Scanned and monitored everything going in and out of agent workspace

- Allowed me to use the same mobile flow I had gotten used to with claude code, but with arbitrary harnesses

I couldn't find a tool that met all of these, so I started bot-bottle. It's evolved into what I'm hoping will be the best security conscious, local first coding agent orchestrator out there.

Here's how it works:

Each agent runs in its own microVM (Firecracker on Linux, Apple's container on macOS, Docker as a weaker fallback), with whichever harness you want. Claude Code, Codex and pi are built in, and custom agent providers are supported (still being documented/tested).

What an agent can reach is defined in a "bottle", which is just a short markdown file listing hosts, repos and which secret goes to which host. Bottles are enforced by a gateway outside the agent VM, which adds the real credentials to requests on the way out, so the agent only sees placeholders. Bottles stack, so you can keep small ones around (npm read only, one repo, one API, etc) and combine them per task. Repos can ship their own bottles, which only run after you trust their exact contents.

Outgoing requests and git pushes are scanned for secrets, and everything is logged locally (you can stream it to your own endpoint as NDJSON or OCSF). Anything a bottle doesn't allow comes to you for approval, in the terminal or on your phone through an optional paired console.

It's in alpha (the console especially), so UI polish is still in progress.

Install:

  curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/diderisoft/bot-bottle/main/install.sh | sh
Docs: https://bot-bottle.com/docs

Would love feedback, especially on the threat model and on whether bottles are the right abstraction.

records.author: unconscionable
records.storyText:
Hey HN! I created a fork of pulumi to explore how we can bring Pulumi's state-journaling architecture to DIY and self-hosted state backends. It's available at https://github.com/ebrake/pulumi-journaling

Background: Pulumi recently detailed their journaling architecture (https://www.pulumi.com/blog/journaling/), which changes how state snapshots are synced. Instead of uploading a massive full state snapshot on every operation (which gets sluggish for large stacks), it streams incremental state operations in parallel, achieving up to 20x speedups.

Journaling optimization has historically been tied to Pulumi Cloud. This repo brings similar state journaling and crash-recovery mechanics (like tracking epoch manifests) that works for file/S3/DIY backends.

I measured these timings against standard OSS pulumi using a GCS rapid bucket (https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/rapid/rapid-bucke...) which has low latency and is inexpensive given the amount of storage usage with a state bucket. Speedups become more effective the more resources you have.

  Resources | Updated | Without journaling | With journaling | Speedup

  ----------+---------+--------------------+-----------------+--------

       24   |  15     | 19.66              | 1.69            | 11.6x

       91   |  50     | 71.36              | 2.12            | 33.7x

      152   |  50     | 70.97              | 1.91            | 37.1x
Would love feedback from anyone else working on IaC state management, concurrency, or crash recovery patterns!

I was finding that managing multiple agent threads with walls of text was getting tiring and inefficient for me and that I wanted a more visual way to interact with my agents, so I built Lynx.

Lynx lets you quickly build fully custom interfaces connected to your data sources (e.g. via MCP or API) and trigger agents running on your machine from them (e.g. with Claude Code or Codex).

I built it as an experiment but have found myself doing 80-90% of my work from inside Lynx. I have my own Conductor-like workspace for coding, a Mail client, a workspace for my writing, and various others for dashboards and explorations.

A few things are really cool about it:

- Adding buttons to a UI that trigger a Claude Code agent running on my machine (e.g. to review a PR, get started on a task from Linear, or look for typos in my text)

- Iterating on the interfaces is really easy, particularly because of a point tool that let's you select what you want changed and an agent will update it live

- Switching between workspaces takes a fraction of a second (much faster than e.g. switching between websites)

- It's all local :)

Harnesses have been moving towards native support for artifacts and MCP-UI which kind of go in this direction but I think the current models add to context fragmentation rather than actually help it, so I flipped the model on its head and built an AI workspace / harness where interactive interfaces are at the core.

Calling this an AI workspace for now but honestly unsure what the proper term should be. Is this a visual harness? A hub for personal software?

Keen to hear feedback about the conceptual model and what others have done that might be similar!

records.title: Show HN: Rowbly – A Software Factory Manager
records.author: _fat_santa
records.storyText:
Hey everyone,

I've been very interested in software factories lately but every time I've read about them, I see folks talking alot about high level concepts and the idea of a software factory but never actually walk you through how to set one up. Or if they do walk you through how to set one up, it's always overly complicated and requires a ton of up-front investment to get things running. In response to this I built rowbly, a CLI that tries to make it as easy as possible to understand and setup a software factory.

Rowbly at it's core works like a kanban board and each column can contain an optional prompt that instructs an agent what to do when a story is within this column. Once you have some stories on your board you run a supervisor skill that monitors the board for changes and spawns agents to work on stories within each column.

The default configuration ships with 5 columns: backlog, refinement, development, review and done. Once a story is moved into refinement, the supervisor automatically dispatches an agent to refine the story based on the instructions in that column. When refinement is finished the ticket is automatically pushed into the development column when another agent is spawned, then into review and finally into done when the PR is merged.

While this is a default configuration, things can get much more exotic based on how things are setup. Each column prompt will define where the story goes after it's finished in that column, so you could wire up a very sophisticated setup, review loops, security scans, testing, etc.

From a data perspective I tried to keep things as simple as possible, all data is stored in plain markdown and json files in the folder where you initialize rowbly.

If you're interested you can run it directly with npx using: `npx rowbly` or install globally with `npm install -g rowbly`. When you run it for the first time, it will walk you through adding stages, prompts and companion skills but all of this can be modified to your liking.

records.title: Show HN: DeployAngel – A verdict in ~20 minutes if a deploy broke production
records.author: jkowens
records.storyText:
Hey there, I'm looking for feedback on a release verification tool I'm building.

https://www.deployangel.com

I decided to build this after an issue popped up with a recent Rails upgrade. We upgraded a Rails app to 8.1 and picked up a new default that changes the order after_commit callbacks run. Our upload code started telling the virus scanner about files before they were saved to S3, and the scanner just quietly dropped them. No exceptions were raised and uploads sat in "processing" for days. We should have had alarms in place, we know that now but I wondered if there could be some type monitoring that would just have noticed the change. I did some checking and the callback route went from roughly 27 requests an hour to zero when we deployed. That seems like a fairly easy change in behavior to automatically raise an alarm. So after a few weekends working with Claude I have a new tool.

A small agent sends one aggregated payload per minute. Then the server compares each release with the last one it cleared. It looks at things like error rates, latency per route, traffic that collapses, and missing job runs. The server then returns a verdict if the release cleared or not. Currently I have agents for Rails, Django, FastAPI, and ASP.NET Core.

It will work best for teams that deploy often and the app gets steady traffic. It's not meant to replace error monitoring tools like Sentry, but to work alongside them. Here's a recent release of its own: https://app.deployangel.com/share/KAaurrfRHcw43ZrjkWst2DLY?r...

The agents are MIT-licensed. It's completely free right now, with a free tier planned.

https://github.com/DeployAngel

I'm looking for a few teams to run it on a real app for a couple of weeks. I'd love to hear if it surfaces issues that other monitoring and alarms miss. Of course I'm hoping it proves to be useful, but if not, that's good information too.

It started in 2019 as a ~200-line script to fix a personal problem: my disk was always full on my potato-puter because of the same directories. Seven years and 45 releases later, I've discovered that node_modules was only part of the problem. Every ecosystem leaves its own pile behind.

So 1.0 replaces the single `target` (node_modules by default) with profiles, which group multiple targets by ecosystem. The default is node (node_modules, .next, .nx, .angular, coverage...), and there are many build-in like Python, Rust or Unity available for use.

To detect certain environments with generic names such as “target”, we check for conditions such as whether there is a `pom.xml` file in the directory, or whether “.venv” contains a `pyvenv.cfg` file.

There are a lots of new changes (multi-select, filters, config file..), which I’ve described in my post: https://zaldih.com/en/post/npkill-1-0-0/

records.title: Show HN: MergeMax, a monthly ranking of public merged PRs on GitHub
records.author: diancodes
records.storyText:
Hi HN, the main idea around MergeMax is that the user can look themselves up and compare themselves against all the other people on the board. No sign-in required. We currently support monthly and daily leaderboards.

I built MergeMax since I kept seeing people post on X about @poteto's merge count and I knew I could probably create something to easily see her and other popular dev's GitHub public PRs. I quickly found out however that her PRs aren't visible via our methods, since most of her PRs are private/not on GitHub. I also wanted to create a place where people can easily see the amount of merges top accounts do each month, now that agents have the ability to create thousands of PRs themselves.

Currently we only support public PRs as well as the contribution total that gets provided by GitHub directly:

- A public PR only counts if it's public, merged, and authored by the account that's being looked up, and merged within the specified period.

- I use GitHub's search API for PR counts. In a single GraphQL query we ask for 1 day per alias (is:pr is:merged is:public author:X merged:DATE), a whole month costs about 1 rate-limit point. If we had to page through PRs it would cost about 400 points per busy account.

- Initially I tried GH Archive first, but PR events there no longer say whether a PR was merged.

Current limitations include:

- People that merged their own PRs also count.

- Agent workflows can increase a person's PR count by a lot. So a bot can generate thousands of small PRs.

- Private work and pushes directly to main don't show as public PRs. Those profiles do, however, show up in GitHub's contribution count if they've activated private contributions on GitHub.

I had to seed about 1,000 accounts at launch and anyone who's been looked up since is also tracked. We obviously cannot track every single account on GitHub.

It really became one of my most fun projects to work on. Especially loved creating the colorscheme/theme. Itterating through top 3 leaderboard designs, user profile look & feel, etc.

I do support sponsor cards like some other popular similar sites but we don't have any sponsors yet.

The stack I used was Tanstack Start deployed to Vercel with Convex as the backend.

I'm open to any questions and feedback regarding the site, how it functions etc. Also would love to hear what you would like to see added to profiles, new boards, etc?

records.author: brendanperry
records.storyText:
Background: My wife and I have 4 boys 4 and under, so we have to get them out of the house consistently to stay sane. Finding good places to take them can be a frustrating process that involves digging through Facebook groups and Google/Yelp reviews that aren't always relevant for parents.

The idea: An app that has reviews of places to take your kids by parents. No AI generated magic, just real people documenting their experience. Sproutings has a map of places parents have been with some ideas for new places to try. You can also coordinate outings with other parents using an outing planning tool.

The challenge: I sat on this idea for a long time because of the challenge that is mapping data. The best POI source you can think of is Google, but their terms are unfriendly and prices don't work for an indie dev. Other better priced options still do not let you store the POI data from their API in your own database. I was determined to have my own map view of all of the places people have reviewed, so I needed coordinates.

The tech: My solution to this was a postgres database full of data I imported and filtered from OSM. This gives me full control over the data to with what I want. So now I have a really cool map view with pins that can scale to millions with no problem using pmtiles. The client side is built with React Native. This was just so I could easily launch on web and mobile. On web, RN has a hard time with SEO, so I had to display some raw HTML / CSS here and there. There are also plenty of challenges with bugs that would only appear on certain platforms, so keeping everything aligned was a constant game of whack-a-mole.

Conclusion: I have a picture in my mind of a Sproutings map overflowing with places reviewed by parents, but the reality is that we have a chicken and egg problem. A platform that relies on user engagement to provide value isn't valuable until people have engaged. However, I'm hoping that I can reach more and more parents that would find it valuable and continue to expand its reach.

I'd love to hear of any and all feedback! Thanks for reading.

Hi HN,

this is Collection of Beauty, a walkable, multi-floor 3D museum, based on a collection of art that I handpicked with 4000+ works.

History: I've spent some time earlier this year just browsing Wikipedia public domain art for literally hours on end, downloading everything that I liked or appreciated, just asking myself do I find this beautiful on some level?

In the end I had a large folder with a bunch of images in it that begged the question: can I make this more useful somehow? Like, it's nice to have all these images sitting on my hard disk somehow but I want to share this with other people as a Collection of Beauty. But they were just images, nothing else.

A bit of wrangling with AI later and now this website exists. It has a 3D museum you can walk through, with multiple floors. The images are displayed at their real sizes relative to one another and the room layouts etc. And yes, the Mona Lisa is that small ^^

Luckily Wikimedia file names can be reverse searched and therefore I had access to the entire Wikimedia metadata against each of the images to sort them and create a metadata catalogue that allows for different ways of slicing through the images, like showing things like: "similar artists", "other artists the artist knew personally", or just "epoch/style" related ideas. I also sorted paintings by color on one of the sub pages, because I thought that would be nifty.

If you find something that is clearly in the wrong epoch or by the wrong artist or the wrong size, has a wrong title or whatever, please file an issue on GitHub (https://github.com/trebeljahr/collection-of-beauty).

Also I know of this other project that did something similar (though they mapped literally all art that ever existed), but I swear I had this idea on my own, sometimes different people come up with the same stuff. https://artmuseum.artfrompixels.com/ When a friend sent this to me, I took some inspiration though and made the frames and lighting and general 3D experience much more beautiful as well. I also had to facepalm myself and whisper: "why didn't I think of this myself," and then added some (public domain or freely licensed) music playing in the background as you look at the paintings.

The whole thing is deployed with Cloudflare workers because it's 90% static and Cloudflare has very very generous free tiers.

Also credit where credit is due, the set of flowers from Redoute is from https://www.c82.net/redoute/ one of my favorite websites of all time ^^

Under the hood the image rendering in the 3D walkthrough does something cool with LOD texture variants where rooms determine when to load each painting's resolution based on a bunch of heuristics, keeping the experience relatively lightweight and fast (hopefully). It should load the really big scans only if you jam up your nose right into a painting.

If some beautiful but more modern art is missing (MC Escher?!) then this is because of copyright issues. There are quite a few artists whose work I would love to include in here but where there is still copyright on the images and therefore I can't afaik.

Also, if you have more Public Domain art, that you personally really like, please share that with me too, would love to include more stuff in here (if I like it ofc ^^). Link to Wikipedia, name of the artist to check out, name of the painting, etc.

I run Claude Code on long tasks and walk away. When I come back, the one thing it needed from me is usually the last line of a long reply, three replies up, or it only ever said it in its thinking.

Handoffs gives those asks a fixed shape. Claude ends its reply with a short block that has a title, what it needs, why it can't do it itself, the steps, the command to run, and the choices. The mod turns that block into a card in a side pane, with checkboxes for the steps, Open and Copy buttons, and a button for each choice. Copy puts the command on your clipboard and never runs it. Open cards go back into the conversation after compaction, so Claude remembers what it's waiting on.

It makes no network calls. Cards stay on your machine and clear themselves after 14 days. MIT licensed. It needs Claude Code 2.1.299 or later and works best in /tui fullscreen.
